LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS: FOOD & HOME · AGES 12–18 MONTHS

Sock — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

The sock card comes with two games built in: dressing and peek-a-boo. This lesson runs both — word at the foot, word at the hand-puppet — and lets the giggles do the gluing.

What is this?

A sock is the soft, stretchy foot-covering your toddler wears, pulls off and occasionally wears on a hand. The card shows a sock; your laundry pile supplies the population. Few words this age come with so much handling built in.

What does it mean?

Clothing words come round every day — sock, shoe, coat — and each rehearsal happens right on the changing mat. The sock also doubles as a toy: stretched over a hand it becomes a puppet, and puppet games make words unforgettable.

What does the child need to know?

Name it at the moment of use: "Sock. On goes the sock." Then the bonus game — sock over your hand, "peek!" — and the same word covers both. One word, two games, double the glue.

Why this matters

Dressing-table words are among the most-repeated a toddler hears, which makes them high-probability early words. The sock’s stretchiness also gives busy fingers a workout — pulling, stretching, poking are hand-skills in disguise.

What it teaches

Clothing vocabulary through routine, fine motor work (pulling, stretching, poking), peek-a-boo as object-permanence practice, and word learning through repeated games.

Words to learn

socktoepullstretchpeeksoft

Say this to your child

“"Sock! A soft little sock. On goes the sock — toes hidden! Pull, pull — off comes the sock. And look: the sock is a puppet now. Peek-a-boo, says the sock. One sock, two games, and the best giggles in the laundry."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card at dressing time, sock in hand: "Sock. On goes the sock."
  2. Name it as it lands: "Sock on! Toes hidden." Then enjoy the foot wiggle that follows — every toddler answers a covered foot with a kick.
  3. Play the pull-off: let your toddler tug the sock free — "off comes the sock!" — and name the ending they engineered.
  4. Stretch the sock over your hand: "Peek-a-boo! The sock says peek." Same word, second game, guaranteed laugh.
  5. Offer the sock to your toddler’s hand for a puppet round of their own, and let the game run until it dissolves — that dissolution is the finish line, not a failure.

Look closer at the picture

The artwork is a sock, soft and stretchy-looking, plain on the card. Name it, then bring out the live one: the card cannot be pulled over a hand, and the hand-puppet version is where this word gets its laugh track.

Ask your child

Watch the two games: does the pull-off or the peek earn the bigger laugh, and does the word get tried at either? Wonder aloud: "I wonder whether you think the sock is clothing or theatre." The honest answer is both.

What your child can say or do

A sock yanked off and held up like a trophy, "sah" or "sok" attempted at the change table, the puppet sock patted or kissed, or a sock worn proudly on the hand all morning — at this age, wearing it wrong is still wearing the word.

Out in the real world

Socks are everywhere: the laundry basket, the drawer, the odd one under the sofa, the pairs on everybody else’s feet. Naming them on sight turns housework into a language walk.

Try it together

Sock matching: two pairs of baby socks, mixed up — find the twins together and name each match "sock, sock!". Matching play is the 12–18-month specialty, and laundry made it first.

Understanding check

Parent self-check: did the naming happen during a real dressing moment, and did the puppet game happen at least once? Routine and play — the two ways this word gets glue.

Parent tips

Follow the fun: if the puppet game beats the dressing lesson, the puppet wins — the word is the same in both. Single socks lost to the sofa monster are fine; the word does not need the pair.

Staying safe

Keep socks out of mouth range at play — the stretchy kind compacts alarmingly — and check the puppet sock for loose threads. The card stays clear of the changing table; changing tables and paper have a feud going.

This lesson pairs with the Sock flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).
